_readme: Five KPI definitions ready to register in Haya's semantic layer + MIRU detectors. Field shapes verified directly against platform/modalities/miru/contracts/metric_semantic_intent.py (MiruMetricSemanticIntentV1 / MiruMetricPublishEnvelopeV1) and the detector plugin source in platform/modalities/miru/detectors/plugins/*.py in github.com/sridharsanta/haya-v1.2. 'detector' is not part of Haya's own intent schema — it's this project's shorthand for the MIRU detector definition to attach to each semantic metric once registered; adapt to whatever object shape MIRU's definition-publish API actually expects.

detector.rationale: Raw sampled metric with a stable-ish daily pattern per device — Z-score against a rolling 30-day mean/std is the direct analogue of the 'capacity watch' card already shipping in the dashboard, just computed server-side and scheduled instead of client-side on every page load.

Field only landed in system_telemetry_metrics_v2 mid-audit — same shape as cpu_usage_pct (raw sampled %, stable-ish daily pattern per device), so the same detector config applies directly, no new plugin needed. Notable: the device this would flag first (NHL100002, P95 95% vs. fleet ~65%) is the exact same device the CPU detector already flags — register both and a downstream correlation step gets a two-metric confirmation on the same device for free, rather than two independent single-metric alerts a human has to notice are about the same machine.

direction=UP only — a faster boot is never worth alerting on, only a slower one. training_window widened to 90D (vs. 30D for CPU/memory) because boot events are inherently sparse: ~29 events/device over 6.5 weeks in the pilot, roughly one every 1.5 days, so P1D grain will have long empty stretches and needs more calendar time to accumulate a stable baseline than a continuously-sampled metric. Register logon_time_total as a second, identical entry alongside this one (same dataset, same detector shape, measure_key='logon_time_total') rather than trying to fold both into one metric — they're independent enough in the pilot data (NHL100002 leads on both, but not by the same margin: 28% slower boot vs. 33% slower logon) that collapsing them would blur which phase is actually degraded. Consider evaluating this metric on a weekly cron rather than daily, since most days won't have a new data point to score.

This is the metric behind the 'NHL100003 RTT climbed 44x' finding — a genuine trend/drift, not just noise around a flat mean. ETS (Holt-Winters) forecasts the expected value and flags residuals, which catches gradual drift that a static Z-score baseline would wash out. Needs >=14 daily points per device to train — thin in the current 8-device pilot, solid at production volume.

derived_measure_definition.note: NOT a raw column on events_v2 — autoheal_failure_rate must be registered in Haya's own metric registry as a computed ratio before this intent resolves to anything. Definition below is what the registration should encode; write it in whatever measure-DSL Haya's semantic model actually uses (Volume 3B's calculated-measure pattern, e.g. crash_rate = 100 * SUM(crashes) / NULLIF(SUM(device_hours),0), is the same shape).
derived_measure_definition.denominator: COUNT(*) WHERE event_type = 'autoheal_action' AND event_status IN ('completed', 'failed')

detector.rationale: This is the metric behind the 'Auto-heal succeeds 100% at Downtown, 0% elsewhere' finding. direction=UP only, since we only care about failure rate spiking, not dropping. deviationFactor=2 (looser than the default 3) because remediation reliability regressions are worth flagging earlier than a generic outlier.

derived_measure_definition.note: Derived per (machine_id, compliance_control, week): percentage of scans in a 'good' status. Good-status mapping already lives in dashboards/app.js as COMPLIANCE_GOOD — reuse it verbatim so the dashboard and the Haya detector never disagree on what 'compliant' means.
derived_measure_definition.formula: 100 * COUNT(*) WHERE compliance_status IN good_status_map[compliance_control] / COUNT(*)

detector.training_window: not applicable — static threshold, no training step
detector.rationale: This is the metric behind the 'NHL100005 non-compliant for 5+ consecutive weeks' finding. Compliance is a policy question, not a statistical one — a fixed 90% floor (configurable per customer) is more defensible to an auditor than 'flag if it looks unusual'. Note threshold-detector's direction values are lowercase ('below'), unlike statistical/ets which use uppercase — verified from source, an easy typo to make.

Crash counts are sparse and low-volume (58 total across 8 devices over ~6 weeks in the pilot as of the latest count, up from 30 at first check — this table is still actively growing) — a Z-score baseline is unstable at that volume (small denominators swing wildly), and 26 of the 58 sit on one device (NHL100006), which would itself skew a fleet-wide mean/std. Percentage-change-vs-prior-period is more robust at low sample counts: flags 'crashes this week are >50% above last week' without needing a stable mean/std first. Revisit in favor of statistical-detector once crash volume is high enough per slice for a stable baseline (rule of thumb: reconsider above ~30 events/device/window).
